title: ASCII has 128 characters because it uses 7 bits
summary: Seven bits give 2 to the 7 = 128 codes: 33 control codes and 95 printable characters.

beats.say: ASCII has exactly one hundred twenty eight characters.
Each one is stored in seven bits.
Seven bits make one hundred twenty eight patterns.
The first thirty three are control codes.
The other ninety five are printable.
Digits, letters and punctuation fill those ninety five.
A byte has eight bits, so one is spare.

data.label: 7 bits + 1 spare
data.flip_label: The spare bit doubles the codes

beats.say: Extended sets used it for more characters.
One more bit doubles the count.
Seven bits, one hundred twenty eight characters.

claims.note: MDN, ASCII: the first 33 code points are non-printing control codes
MDN, ASCII: the other 95 are printable characters

facts.claim: ASCII uses 7 bits to represent 128 characters; the first 33 code points are non-printing control codes and the other 95 are printable characters
facts.note: MDN Glossary, ASCII: '7-bit to represent 128 characters'; first 33 control codes, other 95 printable

facts.claim: When computers standardized on eight-bit bytes the unused eighth bit doubled the code space: ASCII stays the lower half and 8-bit sets add up to 128 more characters, 256 in all
facts.note: Wikipedia, Extended ASCII: of the 2^7 = 128 codes, 33 controls and 95 printable; the eighth bit doubled the code space
